blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Import and export operations, at executive level, are not clerical activities — they are vehicles for allocating risk between sophisticated parties with very different capabilities. Who holds the customs risk? Who holds the FX risk? Who holds the freight risk? Who holds the political risk? Each question has an answer hidden in the contract, often set years ago by people who did not realise they were making strategic decisions.

The senior review asks two uncomfortable questions. First, are we holding risks that our counterparts are better placed to manage, simply because nobody ever renegotiated the terms? Second, are we passing risks to partners who cannot actually absorb them if things go wrong — in which case we are not really transferring the risk, only delaying the moment when it becomes ours again anyway?

Good import and export contracts are living instruments. They are reviewed as capabilities evolve, not only at renewal. The teams that understand this live through disruptions that quietly destroy their competitors, and most of the work happens years before the disruption, in conversations nobody outside the room will ever see.

items.q: According to the text, at executive level import and export operations are best understood as…
options: vehicles for allocating risk between parties
a way of reducing overall freight costs
clerical activities requiring careful paperwork
a compliance obligation imposed by regulators
items.why: "they are vehicles for allocating risk between sophisticated parties" — a tese central.

items.q: Why does the text say the answers to the risk questions are often "hidden in the contract"?
options: Because terms were set years ago by people unaware they were making strategic decisions
Because regulators rarely allow them to be disclosed
Because the contracts are deliberately kept secret
Because only the legal team is permitted to read them
items.why: "set years ago by people who did not realise they were making strategic decisions."

items.q: According to the text, what is the danger of passing a risk to a partner who cannot absorb it?
options: The freight cost will immediately increase
Regulators will treat it as a customs violation
The risk is not really transferred — it returns to you later
The partner will refuse the contract outright
items.why: "we are not really transferring the risk, only delaying the moment when it becomes ours again."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Once signed, a trade contract needs attention only at renewal.
A trade contract should be revisited as capabilities change.
Risk allocation is a genuinely strategic decision.
Some disruptions are survived because of work done years earlier.
items.why: Inferência: o texto insiste que os contratos são "living instruments… reviewed as capabilities evolve, not only at renewal".

items.q: What does the final line — "in conversations nobody outside the room will ever see" — suggest?
options: Disruptions are impossible to prepare for in advance
Only senior executives are allowed into trade negotiations
The most valuable trade work is invisible and happens well before any crisis
Import decisions must be kept confidential for legal reasons
items.why: Inferência: o preparo decisivo ocorre discretamente, anos antes da disrupção — não é visível de fora.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Charlotte apresentar as conclusões da revisão de contratos à diretoria. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
So, we've now been through all twenty agreements, and I want to be candid about what we found. On paper, most of these contracts look prudent — we appear to have pushed the difficult risks onto our partners. The problem is that several of those partners simply cannot carry what we handed them.

Take the two smaller freight forwarders in the eastern corridor. If a shipment is seized at the border, the contract says the loss sits with them. But neither of them has the balance sheet to absorb a claim of that size. So in practice, the moment it goes wrong, they fold, and the exposure lands right back on us — only later, and messier.

What strikes me is that none of this was decided deliberately. These terms were copied forward from older agreements, renewal after renewal, and nobody ever asked whether the counterpart had changed. That's the real finding here. We haven't been allocating risk; we've been inheriting it.

My recommendation is that we reopen four of these before the next cycle, and from now on we treat every renewal as a fresh conversation about who is genuinely best placed to hold each risk — not a rubber stamp on last year's wording.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What did Charlotte find when she reviewed the twenty agreements?
options: The freight costs were far higher than budgeted
On paper the risks looked well placed, but several partners cannot carry them
The contracts had transferred too little risk to partners
All twenty contracts needed to be cancelled immediately
items.why: "most of these contracts look prudent… The problem is that several of those partners simply cannot carry what we handed them."

items.q: What is the problem with the two smaller freight forwarders?
options: They demanded a higher freight rate
They lack the balance sheet to absorb a large claim
They operate outside the eastern corridor
They refused to sign the renewal terms
items.why: "neither of them has the balance sheet to absorb a claim of that size."

items.q: According to Charlotte, how did these risky terms come about?
options: They were imposed by the customs authority
They were negotiated carefully by the board
They were chosen to reduce insurance premiums
They were copied forward from older agreements without review
items.why: "These terms were copied forward from older agreements, renewal after renewal."

items.q: What does Charlotte mean by "We haven't been allocating risk; we've been inheriting it"?
options: The board inherited the contracts from a previous merger
The partners inherited all the company's obligations
The company deliberately keeps every risk on its own books
The risk decisions were never actively made — they simply carried over
items.why: Inferência: "inheriting" = os riscos passaram adiante por inércia, sem decisão consciente de alocação.

items.q: How would you best describe Charlotte's stance?
options: Alarmed but passive, offering no way forward
Indifferent to which party holds the risk
Reassuring — she believes the contracts are basically sound
Critical of the pattern, but proposing a concrete change
items.why: Inferência: ela expõe a falha com franqueza, mas recomenda reabrir contratos e mudar a lógica de renovação.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Treating export contracts as merely clerical is how firms lose money." Here clerical means…
options: financially risky
routine administrative or paperwork-based
legally binding and enforceable
highly strategic and board-level
items.why: Clerical = burocrático, de rotina administrativa — o oposto de estratégico.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "When the peso moved twelve per cent overnight, the desk realised nobody had been assigned the ___."
options: political risk
freight risk
FX risk
customs risk
items.why: Movimento de moeda = FX risk (risco cambial).

items.q: "Our counterpart in Rotterdam agreed to hold the freight risk." A counterpart is…
options: the other party in the agreement
a junior member of the team
an internal auditor
a government regulator
items.why: Counterpart = contraparte, a outra parte do contrato.

items.q: "A supplier that small cannot absorb a claim of that size." To absorb a loss means to…
options: pass it on to a third party
insure against it in advance
report it to the regulator
take it on and bear the cost
items.why: To absorb = absorver, arcar com o custo sem repassá-lo.

items.q: "These clauses are living instruments, not fixed documents." A living instrument is best described as…
options: an informal, non-binding memo
a contract signed by living directors
a contract that is revised as circumstances change
a permanent, unchangeable agreement
items.why: Living instrument = instrumento vivo, revisado à medida que as capacidades evoluem.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em revisões de contratos de comércio exterior. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Legal still has to sign off on the reallocated clauses." To sign off on means to…
options: comment informally
translate into another language
formally approve
postpone indefinitely
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Two forwarders pushed back on taking the customs risk." They…
options: resisted or challenged the proposal
accepted it without objection
rewrote the whole contract
delayed reading the terms
items.why: Push back on = resistir, contestar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "We need to follow through on the renegotiation before renewal." To follow through means to…
options: mention it in passing
carry it to completion
delegate it to another office
abandon it halfway
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado.

items.q: "Reopening four contracts won't move the needle unless we change the renewal process." This means it will…
options: take too long to measure
not make a meaningful difference
cost more than expected
create legal exposure
items.why: Move the needle = fazer diferença perceptível; aqui, sozinho não muda o quadro.

items.q: "If a shipment is seized, the smaller partner would simply walk away from the claim." To walk away from means to…
options: abandon the obligation and leave it unpaid
pay it in instalments
appeal to the authorities
negotiate a lower settlement
items.why: Walk away from = abandonar a obrigação, deixando o risco recair sobre a outra parte.
